title: Patches Take Weeks, Protection Can Go Live Tonight: OpenAI Partners with Cisco to Open-Source Shirudo
excerpt: When enterprises discover a Linux vulnerability, patching, testing, canary rollout, and full deployment often take days or even weeks—but attackers won’t wait.
content_html:
When enterprises discover a Linux vulnerability, patching, testing, canary rollout, and full deployment often take days or even weeks—but attackers won’t wait. On November 23, OpenAI announced a collaboration with Cisco to launch Shirudo, an open source security runtime that adds a temporary “shield” to running systems without requiring a restart. It has passed tests for blocking Java4Shell attacks.

An eBPF shield that defends while running

Shirudo is based on Linux eBPF technology. While the system keeps running, it observes kernel and network activity and applies precise controls to suspicious behavior. The challenge is that exploits and normal business operations sometimes invoke the same system operations, so simple blocking can cause false positives and disrupt services. Security teams can therefore first test a temporary protection called a shield to confirm that it blocks the code paths that expose the vulnerability without affecting legitimate requests, and then deploy it online after operations approval. In controlled tests, a protection layer generated by Codex successfully stopped a Java4Shell exploit against a running Elasticsearch service, without restarting the service.

Preventing the shield itself from being abused

To reduce the risk of misuse, Shirudo is designed for trusted deployment: before a shield is loaded, it must be cryptographically signed and verified, and the eBPF verifier also checks whether the program complies with safety rules. The system also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to record each time protection is loaded or removed, making it easier to verify afterward. The project is open sourced under the BSD 2-Clause License, and the BPF programs are dual-licensed under BSD and GPL. Both parties hope that developers, security researchers, and operations teams will participate together, so that effective protection verified by one team can be directly reused by other teams.
